clinical_knowledge.topic: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus with Lupus Nephritis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus with Lupus Nephritis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes hydroxychloroquine and timely immunosuppressive therapy for active organ-threatening disease, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: butterfly facial rash, joint pains, mouth ulcers, and frothy urine in young woman

Key HPI features: 27F presents with 3-month history of a red, sunburn-like rash across her cheeks and nose that spares the nasolabial folds (malar rash) and worsens after sunlight exposure. Reports migratory polyarthralgias in fingers/knees, painless oral ulcers on the hard palate, severe fatigue, and new-onset foamy, bubbly urine.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 140/90. Classic malar erythematous rash across bridge of nose and cheeks sparing nasolabial folds. Painless palatal ulcers. Non-erosive tenderness in MCPs and wrists. Urinalysis: 3+ protein, 2+ blood, RBC casts present. 24-hour urine protein reveals 2.8 g/day. Bloods: ANA positive 1:1280 (homogeneous), Anti-dsDNA strongly positive (1:320), Anti-Smith positive, Complement C3 and C4 markedly suppressed, Serum Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (up from 0.8 baseline).
Relevant background/PMH: Raynaud's phenomenon for 2 years
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Systemic Lupus Erythematosus with Lupus Nephritis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Rheumatoid arthritis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Missing active nephritis with rising creatinine, hematuria/casts, hypertension, edema, or oliguria; this needs urgent nephrology and rheumatology assessment.
management_principles: Urgently involve nephrology and rheumatology for suspected active lupus nephritis; confirm severity and usually obtain a kidney biopsy when safe before selecting induction treatment.
Hydroxychloroquine and glucocorticoids may be appropriate but require clinician-directed dosing, retinal monitoring, infection-risk assessment, and pregnancy counseling.

Choose mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, or other induction therapy by biopsy class and patient factors; counsel on infection, fertility/pregnancy risks, contraception where relevant, vaccines, and laboratory monitoring.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 27F presenting with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) flare with photosensitive malar rash, oral ulcers, polyarthralgia, and signs of lupus nephritis (foamy urine).
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 140/90. Classic malar erythematous rash across bridge of nose and cheeks sparing nasolabial folds. Painless palatal ulcers. Non-erosive tenderness in MCPs and wrists. Urinalysis: 3+ protein, 2+ blood, RBC casts present. 24-hour urine protein reveals 2.8 g/day. Bloods: ANA positive 1:1280 (homogeneous), Anti-dsDNA strongly positive (1:320), Anti-Smith positive, Complement C3 and C4 markedly suppressed, Serum Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (up from 0.8 baseline).
reference_soap.assessment: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) complicated by active Lupus Nephritis (likely Class III/IV proliferative).
reference_soap.plan: 1. Arrange urgent nephrology and rheumatology assessment for active nephritis and blood-pressure/renal-function management; obtain a kidney biopsy when safe to guide treatment. 2. A clinician should determine hydroxychloroquine, glucocorticoid, and induction immunosuppression after assessing infection, pregnancy/fertility plans, renal function, and contraindications. 3. Monitor urine protein/sediment, creatinine, blood pressure, blood counts, liver function, complement/anti-dsDNA as clinically indicated; seek emergency care for oliguria, worsening edema, severe headache, breathlessness, fever, or confusion.

learning_objectives: Identify clinical and immunological diagnostic criteria for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
Recognize hypocomplementemia (low C3/C4) and rising anti-dsDNA titers as markers of active lupus flare/nephritis
Enforce universal baseline prescription of Hydroxychloroquine with retinal monitoring in SLE management
Coordinate urgent renal biopsy and induction therapy (Mycophenolate vs Cyclophosphamide) for lupus nephritis

teaching.diagnosis: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus with Lupus Nephritis
teaching.one_liner: A multisystem autoimmune disease causing a sun-sensitive malar rash, joint pain, and oral ulcers; kidney involvement may cause foamy urine and requires urgent specialist evaluation for biopsy-guided treatment.
red_flags: Foamy urine with leg swelling, reduced urine output, rising blood pressure, blood in the urine, or worsening fatigue may signal active nephritis and needs urgent assessment.
Severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness, confusion, fever, or rapidly worsening swelling warrants emergency evaluation.

must_ask.say: Does the rash on your face get worse after being in the sun?
Which joints hurt, and does the pain move around?
Have you had any mouth sores?
Has your urine looked foamy or bubbly?
Do your fingers turn white or blue in the cold?

history.answer: I've had this red rash across my cheeks and nose for about three months, and my fingers and knees have been aching.
The redness started on both cheeks about three months ago and gradually spread across the bridge of my nose.
It sits right over my cheeks and nose, and it flares up and gets much redder whenever I spend time in the sunlight.
It looks like a red sunburn shaped like a butterfly, but the skin folds around my nose and mouth are totally clear.
It doesn't really itch or hurt, and I didn't have any nerve tingling or burning before it appeared.
No, once it flared up, it stayed constantly on my face rather than coming and going within hours.
I've never had a facial rash like this before in my life, and I haven't received any medical treatment for it yet.
I haven't had a fever or chills, but I've been feeling profoundly exhausted and worn out every single day.
I noticed a couple of shallow sores on the roof of my mouth, but surprisingly they don't cause any pain when I eat.
No, my skin isn't peeling or blistering, and I don't have any dark purple spots that fail to fade.
My throat feels open, my lips and face aren't swollen, and I haven't had any trouble breathing or dizziness.
I haven't started any new prescription drugs, antibiotics, gout medication, or painkillers recently.
I haven't used new cosmetics, detergents, or metal jewelry, and I haven't eaten any unfamiliar foods.
No one in my family or at the school where I teach has any rash or illness like this.
I haven't been bitten by ticks or bugs, and I haven't gone hiking, traveling, or using public baths.
I don't have any history of childhood eczema, asthma, or seasonal allergies.
My finger joints, wrists, and knees ache and feel stiff in the mornings, moving from one joint to another, but my nails look normal.
I put some basic moisturizing facial lotion on my cheeks, but it didn't help at all.
I am in a monogamous relationship with my husband, and I've never had any genital ulcers or sores.
For the past few weeks, my urine has looked noticeably frothy and foamy every time I use the restroom.
Whenever my hands get cold, my fingers turn stark white, then bluish and numb, which has been happening for two years.
I looked up butterfly rashes on the internet and read about lupus, so I suspect that might be what I have.
I'm terrified that lupus might be damaging my kidneys and that I could become critically ill or die young.
I want thorough blood and urine testing done today and to start the right medication immediately.
Other than the color changes in my fingers in the cold, I have no chronic medical conditions.
I've never had any surgeries and I've never been hospitalized.
I don't take any prescription medications, over-the-counter painkillers, or dietary supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only drink an occasional glass of wine once or twice a month, and never heavily.
I work as an elementary school teacher and live in an apartment with my husband.
There is no family history of kidney failure, lupus, or other autoimmune conditions.
My menstrual cycle is regular every twenty-eight days, my last period started two weeks ago, and I am not pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg, heart rate 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Confluent erythematous macular rash across the bridge of the nose and both cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds, with no scaling, crusting, or skin sloughing.
Shallow, non-tender ulcers visible on the hard palate; oral mucosa is otherwise moist and pink.
Tenderness on palpation of the bilateral metacarpophalangeal joints and wrists without joint effusion, warmth, or deformity; range of motion is preserved.
No cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy palpable.
Conjunctivae are pink without injection, discharge, or ulceration; sclerae are anicteric.
Trace bilateral pretibial pitting edema; peripheral pulses are intact and symmetrical.
